event: The Ottoman conquest finds the Samaritans a scattered remnant of ~500, spread across Nablus, Gaza, Damascus, and Cairo.
High Priest Pinḥas is exiled to Damascus — leadership disruption under early Ottoman rule.
Tax-register peak: ~1,400 Samaritans (Nablus ~120–205, Gaza ~48–150, Safed ~30, Cairo ~300) — the high point of the entire Ottoman record.
Murad III dress restrictions — small turbans, no silk — among repeated dhimmi sumptuary firmans.
The Aaronid high-priestly line ends: the last Aaronid, Shelemiah b. Pinḥas, flees Nablus over local disputes and is murdered en route; Levitical priests take over thereafter.
Under the Tuqan and Jarrar governors, Muslims plunder the High Priest's house and the ritual bath and seize houses, vineyards, fields and 'countless goods' — and forcibly convert many Samaritans.
quote: Ils convertirent par force beaucoup de Samaritains. (They forcibly converted many Samaritans.)

event: Sultan Mehmed IV forbids access to Mount Gerizim, forcing the Passover sacrifice onto the mountain's eastern slope — a dated central-authority religious ban.

The Damascus community disappears, substantially by conversion to Islam: several prominent Muslim families of Damascus (Dar Gofari, Dar Nahas, Dar Rumah, Dar Mneid) are of Samaritan origin — the apostasy ratchet visible in family genealogies.
A Jerusalem-mufti fatwa affirms the Samaritans as People of the Book — an intermittent legal floor; they are taxed alongside the Jews.
The Cairo Samaritan synagogue is handed over to the local Jewish community — no Samaritans left in Cairo.
During Napoleon's invasion local Arabs seize the property of the Gaza community; by now the diaspora has contracted to Nablus alone — 'the only place in the entire world' where Samaritans remain.
The wealthy Shelaby / Danfī bankers — the community's de-facto leaders and bankers to the Nablus governors — are repeatedly extorted, arrested, and (1805, 1813) murdered.
Persecution under the governors 'Abdul Hady and Moosa Bek' — named by Mills as an earlier crisis a generation before the 1841 extirpation plot.

The Egyptian decade under Ibrahim Pasha is the one window of relief — in the community's own chronicle, his just and equitable government relieved the Samaritans 'of the tyranny of the peoples inhabiting this country.' An inverted pasha-cascade: here the Egyptian rule itself was the opening, and its end the catastrophe.
quote: …the Samaritans were relieved of the tyranny of the peoples inhabiting this country, for his government was just and equitable.

event: On the Egyptian withdrawal, the Muslim inhabitants of Nablus vent their hatred of the toppled Egyptians in a pogrom against the Samaritans — whose notables had been the visible non-Muslim functionaries of the regime.

The extirpation crisis: the ʿulamāʾ rule the Samaritans 'had no religion at all' — not People of the Book but pagans 'whom every true believer was commanded to convert or exterminate.' A widow's son Isaac is imprisoned, lashed, and forcibly converted (renamed 'Asaad'); her daughter dies of fear of the torture.

Rescue: the Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, Haim Avraham Gagin, issues a written declaration that 'the Samaritan people is a branch of the children of Israel' — refuting the ʿulamāʾ and giving the community just enough theological cover to survive. (The ruling is still cited in Israeli religious-status debates.)

British consular protection: Consul James Finn intervenes; the agent Jacob esh-Shellaby carries a petition to London; Lord Clarendon sends £50 with orders to use 'good offices to save the Samaritan people from persecution, from whatever quarter,' and Stratford de Redcliffe presses the Porte.
Petermann counts ~122 Samaritans — the community is now a single endogamous core at Nablus.
John Mills, living among the community, counts 40 families / ~150 souls in a 'ghetto-like' quarter at the foot of Gerizim (+1 by 1860).
The Ottoman state pacifies the Nablus district by force, breaks the local feudal lords, and installs direct rule — beginning an unaccustomed 'deep peace' that runs to WWI.
The community reaches its all-time low — about 85 souls — with a male-to-female ratio approaching 2:1; extinction is widely forecast and never arrives.
Historic nadir, ~140 souls; the American philanthropist E. K. Warren, 'amazed and enchanted' to find them surviving into the 20th century, builds medical and educational facilities, aiding recovery.
Abraham b. Marḥiv Tsedaka settles in Jaffa (attempts 1894, 1902; success 1905) — the nucleus of the modern second Samaritan centre (later Tel Aviv, then Ḥolon 1951).

The old Nablus synagogue is damaged in the magnitude-6.2 July earthquake — relief in this window came less from any change of heart among neighbours than from restored central order plus outside patronage.
